script.opening: "Doctor, I keep getting these frightening attacks out of nowhere — a pounding headache, my heart races, I pour with sweat and go pale and shaky, with this awful sense of dread. They last a few minutes then pass. And the nurse keeps getting really high, all-over-the-place blood pressure readings. I’m only 39. People keep saying it’s anxiety, but it doesn’t feel like that."

facts.text: For about 6 months, two or three a week. Come out of the blue — at rest, at work, once while straining on the toilet. Pounding headache, heart thumping, soaked in sweat, colleagues say he goes white, hands shake. Lasts 5–15 minutes, then washed out for an hour.
The physical symptoms come first; the dread is part of it, not before it. No worrying thoughts beforehand. Not anxious in between: "I’m fine in between."
Practice nurse readings over 2 months: 168/104, 142/90, 186/112 — "she said they were all over the place". Bought a home monitor: one reading during an attack was 210/120, normal ones about 135/85.

Lost about half a stone without trying. No chest pain, no fainting. No heat intolerance or diarrhoea. Not diabetic as far as he knows. No caffeine binges (2 coffees a day), no energy drinks, no cocaine or amphetamines, no decongestants or slimming pills. Alcohol 6 units a week.
None regularly. A previous GP suggested propranolol "for the anxiety" — he hasn’t started it yet. No allergies.
"Not that I know of." Parents alive and well; no known family history of high blood pressure, tumours or hormone problems.
IT project manager. Married, one daughter. Cycles to work.

Frustrated at being told it’s anxiety; calm and logical in between attacks. If the doctor explores the pattern carefully, warm up. Ask "A growth? Is it cancer?" if a tumour is mentioned. Ask whether you should start the propranolol.

ice.ideas: "Something physical. It just doesn’t feel like nerves."
ice.concerns: "That something’s being missed. And my blood pressure — my heart feels like it’ll burst." Worried about having a stroke.

cues: "People keep saying it’s anxiety, but it doesn’t feel like that" — take the pattern seriously.
"My blood pressure’s all over the place" — labile hypertension in a young man.
"The other GP suggested propranolol" (if medicines are asked) — a beta-blocker alone could be dangerous here.

checkpoints.text: Considers PHAEOCHROMOCYTOMA from the classic paroxysmal triad (headache, palpitations, sweating) with labile/resistant/young-onset HYPERTENSION — rather than assuming essential hypertension or anxiety
Recognises the indications to consider secondary hypertension (paroxysmal symptoms, resistant/young-onset HTN, hypertensive crises, hereditary syndromes)
Distinguishes the mimics (anxiety/panic, hyperthyroidism — TFTs, arrhythmia — ECG, hypoglycaemia, drugs/stimulants) rather than simply labelling it anxiety

Investigates with plasma free METANEPHRINES or 24-hour urinary metanephrines/catecholamines, then imaging if positive, and refers to ENDOCRINOLOGY (same day if clinic BP 180/120 mmHg or higher with suspected phaeochromocytoma, NICE NG136)

Knows the management principle that ALPHA-blockade must precede BETA-blockade (beta first/alone risks a hypertensive crisis), that surgery cures most people but lifelong follow-up is needed, and that hereditary associations exist (MEN2/VHL/NF1/SDH; genetic testing usually offered)
Validates that "it doesn’t feel like anxiety", takes the paroxysmal symptoms and labile BP seriously, and explains the plan without dismissing him
Explains the investigations and referral clearly and checks understanding, balancing thoroughness with reassurance

Safety-nets and follows up: metanephrine testing + endocrinology referral, interim BP/symptom safety-netting (home BP diary; same-day contact if BP 180/120 or higher; severe headache, chest pain, breathlessness or confusion → 999), mimic screening, and review — thinking of the zebra and testing, not just an anxiety label

worked.txt: "I hear you — and you’re right that recurrent attacks like this, with your blood pressure swinging high, deserve more than an ‘anxiety’ label, especially at 39. There’s a specific condition I want to check for."

"That triad — pounding headache, racing heart and drenching sweats in sudden episodes, with high erratic blood pressure — can be caused by a rare hormone-producing growth on the adrenal gland called a phaeochromocytoma. It’s uncommon but important because it’s treatable and usually curable."

"The key test measures hormones called metanephrines — either a blood test or a 24-hour urine collection. I’ll also check your thyroid, kidneys and sugar and do a heart tracing, as those can cause similar symptoms, and I’d like to see you in person to check your blood pressure lying and standing."

"If the test is positive, you’d have a scan to find it and see the hormone specialists. There’s an important detail in treatment — a specific type of blood-pressure medicine has to be started first before others — which the specialists manage."
"This is rare, so it may well turn out not to be this — but it’s exactly the kind of thing we shouldn’t miss, which is why I’m testing rather than just reassuring you."

"While we investigate, if you get a sudden severe headache, chest pain, breathlessness or confusion during an attack, call 999, and contact us the same day if your home blood pressure is 180 over 120 or higher. I’ll arrange the tests and referral and we’ll review the results together."

f.learning: PHAEOCHROMOCYTOMA (a catecholamine-secreting tumour, usually of the adrenal medulla) classically causes PAROXYSMS of the triad — pounding HEADACHE, PALPITATIONS and drenching SWEATING — with pallor, tremor, anxiety/sense of doom, and HYPERTENSION that may be paroxysmal or sustained and is often labile/resistant; the episodic triad with labile BP, especially in a younger patient, should raise the possibility. Consider phaeochromocytoma (and other secondary causes of hypertension) in paroxysmal symptoms, RESISTANT hypertension, YOUNG-ONSET hypertension, hypertensive crises, or a hereditary syndrome, rather than assuming essential hypertension or anxiety — it is rare but important ("the zebra") because it is potentially curable and dangerous if missed. Distinguish the common mimics: anxiety/panic disorder (overlapping symptoms, but phaeochromocytoma has marked objective hypertension/pallor and a stereotyped triad), hyperthyroidism (check TFTs), arrhythmia (ECG), hypoglycaemia, drugs/stimulants and alcohol withdrawal. Investigate biochemically first — plasma free METANEPHRINES or 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines (Endocrine Society 2014, international) with TFTs, U&E, glucose/HbA1c and ECG — and, if positive, the specialist images (CT/MRI of the adrenals ± functional imaging) to localise the tumour, with referral to endocrinology (NICE NG136: specialist evaluation for secondary causes under 40; same-day referral if clinic BP is 180/120 mmHg or higher with suspected phaeochromocytoma). A key management principle (specialist-led) is that ALPHA-blockade must precede BETA-blockade, because giving a beta-blocker first or alone can cause unopposed alpha-mediated vasoconstriction and a hypertensive crisis; definitive treatment is surgical removal, which cures most people, though lifelong follow-up is needed because tumours can recur and a minority are malignant; hereditary associations (MEN2, von Hippel-Lindau, NF1, SDH genes) are common, so genetic testing is usually offered and relatives may need screening. The skill is to think of phaeochromocytoma in the paroxysmal-triad/secondary-hypertension patient, test metanephrines, screen mimics and refer — not just label it anxiety.

knowledge.summary: Sudden attacks of headache, palpitations and sweating, with pallor and high, swinging blood pressure in a man under 40, should make you think of phaeochromocytoma before calling it anxiety. It is rare but curable, and dangerous if missed. Test plasma free or 24-hour urinary metanephrines, check for mimics, and refer to endocrinology. Do not start a beta-blocker. Arrange same-day assessment if blood pressure is very high with symptoms of a crisis.

points.t: Episodes of headache, palpitations and sweating are the classic triad, often with pallor, tremor and a sense of doom, lasting minutes. Blood pressure may be high only during attacks or all the time, and is often labile. Many patients have only some of these features.

Paroxysmal symptoms with hypertension, hypertension under 40, resistant hypertension, a severe rise with anaesthesia or certain drugs, an adrenal incidentaloma, or a family history of a hereditary syndrome. NICE NG136 advises considering specialist evaluation for secondary causes in adults under 40 with hypertension [1], and the British and Irish Hypertension Society sets out a structured work-up for young-onset hypertension [5].

Panic disorder, hyperthyroidism, arrhythmia, hypoglycaemia, stimulants and drugs (including cocaine, amfetamines and decongestants), alcohol withdrawal and carcinoid. Anxiety remains a diagnosis of exclusion when the blood pressure is objectively labile.

Plasma free metanephrines or 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines are the first-line tests [2]; use whichever your laboratory offers. Some medicines, such as tricyclic antidepressants, can cause false positives. Add TFTs, U&E, glucose or HbA1c and an ECG. Do not delay an urgent specialist referral while waiting for results (NICE NG136 [1]); imaging is arranged by the specialist only after positive biochemistry.

A beta-blocker given alone can leave alpha-driven vasoconstriction unopposed and trigger a hypertensive crisis. The BNF lists phaeochromocytoma as a contraindication to beta-blockers unless an alpha-blocker is already in place [3]. The specialist starts alpha-blockade first, for example phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin [4], before surgery.

Refer for same-day specialist assessment if clinic BP is 180/120 mmHg or higher with suspected phaeochromocytoma, for example labile or postural hypotension, headache, palpitations, pallor, abdominal pain or sweating (NICE NG136 [1]). Chest pain, confusion, severe headache or breathlessness during an attack need 999.

Surgical removal after preparation cures most people, but lifelong follow-up is needed because tumours can recur and a minority are malignant. A large share are hereditary (MEN2, von Hippel–Lindau, NF1, SDH genes), so genetic testing is usually offered and relatives may need screening [2].

model.text: Hello Mr Vasquez, I’m Dr Evans. What would you like to talk about today?

I keep getting these frightening attacks out of nowhere. A pounding headache, my heart races, I pour with sweat, go pale and shaky, with an awful sense of dread. They last a few minutes then pass. And the nurse keeps getting really high blood pressure readings that are all over the place. I’m only 39. People keep saying it’s anxiety, but it doesn’t feel like that.

That sounds really frightening, and I can hear you’re fed up with being told it’s anxiety. I’d like to go through the attacks in detail, check your blood pressure, and then talk about what I think we should do. Is that okay?
Yes. That’s what I want.
Talk me through the last attack from start to finish.
It came out of the blue. The headache is like my head’s pounding, my heart thumps, I’m soaked in sweat and people tell me I go white. Then it passes and I feel washed out.
Is there anything that sets them off, such as exercise, bending, straining, certain foods or medicines?
Not that I’ve noticed. They just come.
Before an attack, do you notice worry building up, or does it start with the physical symptoms?
model.why: Separates panic from a physical cause

model.text: The physical stuff comes first. The dread is part of it, not before it.
Have you had any chest pain, fainting, or feeling dizzy when you stand up?
model.why: Screens cardiac symptoms and postural hypotension

model.text: No, not really.
Any weight loss, feeling hot all the time, tremor between attacks, or changes in your bowels?
No, I’m fine in between.
Do you take any medicines, supplements or anything bought over the counter, or use caffeine, energy drinks or recreational drugs?
Nothing I can think of.
Does anyone in your family have blood pressure problems at a young age, adrenal or thyroid tumours, or conditions that run in families?
Not that I know of.
What do you think might be causing this?
I don’t know. Something physical. It just doesn’t feel like nerves.
What worries you most?
That something’s being missed. And my blood pressure. My heart feels like it’ll burst.
And what were you hoping we would do?
Look for the cause properly.
I’ll check your pulse and blood pressure sitting and standing, listen to your heart, feel your neck for your thyroid and look at the back of your eyes.
Go ahead.

I’ll check your blood pressure over time as well. I think you’re right to question the anxiety label. Sudden attacks of headache, racing heart and sweating, with pallor and swinging blood pressure at your age, can be caused by a rare growth on the adrenal gland called a phaeochromocytoma. It releases bursts of adrenaline-like hormones.
A growth? Is it cancer?

It’s usually not cancer, and it’s rare, so this may well turn out to be something else. But it’s important to check for, because it can be cured with an operation, and it can be dangerous if missed. That’s why I want to test rather than reassure.
model.why: Answers the fear honestly and proportionately

model.text: Okay. That makes sense.

The key test measures breakdown products of these hormones, called metanephrines, either in a blood test or a 24-hour urine collection. I’ll also check your thyroid, kidneys and sugar, and do a heart tracing today, because those can cause similar attacks.
And if it’s positive?

Then you’d see the hormone specialists, who arrange a scan to find it. Before any operation they start a particular type of blood pressure tablet first to keep you safe. That’s why I won’t start a beta-blocker today, even though your heart races. On its own it could make things worse if this is the cause.
model.why: Explains alpha-before-beta and avoids a beta-blocker

model.text: So no tablets for now?

Not until we know more, unless your pressure is dangerously high. I’d like you to use a home blood pressure monitor twice a day, and also during an attack if you can, and write down what happened. That helps the specialist too.
model.why: Home monitoring with a symptom diary

model.text: I can do that.

If you get a severe headache that doesn’t settle, chest pain, breathlessness, confusion, weakness or problems with your vision during an attack, call 999. If home readings are 180 over 120 or higher, contact us or NHS 111 the same day. Can you tell me the plan in your own words?

model.text: Blood or urine test for these hormones, thyroid and kidney bloods, heart tracing, home BP with a diary. No beta-blocker. 999 for a severe headache or chest pain.
That’s it exactly. I’ll call you with the results and see you in two weeks, sooner if needed.

social.t: Repeated anxiety labels erode trust. Taking the physical story seriously rebuilds the relationship, whatever the tests show.
Unpredictable attacks can affect work and activities. Explore this and offer a fit note if he cannot work safely while investigated.

legal.t: Hypertension alone does not require a Group 1 driver to notify the DVLA. If attacks cause dizziness or impaired awareness, advise him not to drive during symptoms, and check DVLA guidance if he holds a Group 2 licence.

professional.t: Earlier labels can stop fresh thinking. Reconsidering the diagnosis when the story does not fit is part of safe practice (GMC Good medical practice).
Agree who checks the metanephrine result and how he will hear about it; abnormal results need prompt endocrinology referral.

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed by agreeing with everyone who came before. The marks are for thinking again when the story doesn’t fit.

items.why: The triad with labile BP at 39 needs a secondary cause excluded.
Unopposed alpha stimulation can cause a hypertensive crisis.
items.fix: Avoid beta-blockers until phaeochromocytoma is excluded.

items.why: Hyperthyroidism, arrhythmia and drugs are commoner.
items.fix: TFTs, ECG and a drug and stimulant history.

items.why: A crisis can cause stroke or heart damage.
items.fix: Give BP and symptom thresholds for urgent help (NICE NG136).

items.fail: Dismissing his frustration, or saying ‘tumour’ without context.
items.why: It repeats the harm and frightens him.
items.fix: Validate, then explain honestly and proportionately.

items.why: A positive test needs prompt referral.
items.fix: Agree how results are given and book a review.

points.t: Episodes of headache, palpitations and sweating are the classic triad, often with pallor, tremor and a sense of doom, lasting minutes. Blood pressure may be high only during attacks or all the time, and is often labile. Many patients have only some of these features.

Paroxysmal symptoms with hypertension, hypertension under 40, resistant hypertension, a severe rise with anaesthesia or certain drugs, an adrenal incidentaloma, or a family history of a hereditary syndrome. NICE NG136 advises considering specialist evaluation for secondary causes in adults under 40 with hypertension [1], and the British and Irish Hypertension Society sets out a structured work-up for young-onset hypertension [5].

Panic disorder, hyperthyroidism, arrhythmia, hypoglycaemia, stimulants and drugs (including cocaine, amfetamines and decongestants), alcohol withdrawal and carcinoid. Anxiety remains a diagnosis of exclusion when the blood pressure is objectively labile.

Plasma free metanephrines or 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines are the first-line tests [2]; use whichever your laboratory offers. Some medicines, such as tricyclic antidepressants, can cause false positives. Add TFTs, U&E, glucose or HbA1c and an ECG. Do not delay an urgent specialist referral while waiting for results (NICE NG136 [1]); imaging is arranged by the specialist only after positive biochemistry.

A beta-blocker given alone can leave alpha-driven vasoconstriction unopposed and trigger a hypertensive crisis. The BNF lists phaeochromocytoma as a contraindication to beta-blockers unless an alpha-blocker is already in place [3]. The specialist starts alpha-blockade first, for example phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin [4], before surgery.

Refer for same-day specialist assessment if clinic BP is 180/120 mmHg or higher with suspected phaeochromocytoma, for example labile or postural hypotension, headache, palpitations, pallor, abdominal pain or sweating (NICE NG136 [1]). Chest pain, confusion, severe headache or breathlessness during an attack need 999.

Surgical removal after preparation cures most people, but lifelong follow-up is needed because tumours can recur and a minority are malignant. A large share are hereditary (MEN2, von Hippel–Lindau, NF1, SDH genes), so genetic testing is usually offered and relatives may need screening [2].

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; let him describe the attacks and his frustration at the anxiety label before narrowing.
Explored his fear of something being missed and the effect of the attacks; asked about stimulants and recreational drugs.
Picked up the classic triad, pallor and labile BP at 39, and that physical symptoms come before the dread.
Idea: something physical, not nerves. Concern: being dismissed; his blood pressure. Expectation: a proper search for the cause.
Lying and standing BP, pulse, heart, thyroid and fundi; plasma free or 24-hour urinary metanephrines, TFTs, U&E, glucose or HbA1c, ECG; home BP with symptom diary.
Phaeochromocytoma versus panic disorder, hyperthyroidism, arrhythmia, hypoglycaemia, drugs and stimulants.
Screened chest pain, syncope and postural symptoms; applied NICE NG136 same-day criteria.
Metanephrine testing and endocrinology referral; no beta-blocker; explained the alpha-before-beta principle; home monitoring.
Considered hereditary syndromes and family screening; honest, proportionate answer about cancer.
999 for crisis symptoms; same-day contact if BP 180/120 or higher; results call and review in two weeks.

social.t: Repeated anxiety labels erode trust. Taking the physical story seriously rebuilds the relationship, whatever the tests show.
Unpredictable attacks can affect work and activities. Explore this and offer a fit note if he cannot work safely while investigated.

legal.t: Hypertension alone does not require a Group 1 driver to notify the DVLA. If attacks cause dizziness or impaired awareness, advise him not to drive during symptoms, and check DVLA guidance if he holds a Group 2 licence.

professional.t: Earlier labels can stop fresh thinking. Reconsidering the diagnosis when the story does not fit is part of safe practice (GMC Good medical practice).
Agree who checks the metanephrine result and how he will hear about it; abnormal results need prompt endocrinology referral.

community.t: Charity patient information on phaeochromocytoma and paraganglioma, and genetic counselling services for families if a hereditary cause is found.

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Possible phaeochromocytoma: paroxysms of headache, palpitations and sweating with pallor and labile hypertension at 39. Mimics (panic disorder, hyperthyroidism, arrhythmia, drugs) to be excluded.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Your attacks could be caused by a rare growth on the adrenal gland that releases bursts of adrenaline. It’s usually not cancer and it can be cured with an operation. A blood or urine test will tell us whether we need to look further.”

management.reflectIce: “You told me this doesn’t feel like anxiety, and your blood pressure backs you up. So we’ll look for a physical cause properly.”
management.psychosocial: Validate his experience; fit note if needed; clear communication of results.

No beta-blocker; endocrinology referral if positive; specialist starts alpha-blockade first

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed by agreeing with everyone who came before. The marks are for thinking again when the story doesn’t fit.

items.why: The triad with labile BP at 39 needs a secondary cause excluded.
Unopposed alpha stimulation can cause a hypertensive crisis.
items.fix: Avoid beta-blockers until phaeochromocytoma is excluded.

items.why: Hyperthyroidism, arrhythmia and drugs are commoner.
items.fix: TFTs, ECG and a drug and stimulant history.

items.why: A crisis can cause stroke or heart damage.
items.fix: Give BP and symptom thresholds for urgent help (NICE NG136).

items.fail: Dismissing his frustration, or saying ‘tumour’ without context.
items.why: It repeats the harm and frightens him.
items.fix: Validate, then explain honestly and proportionately.

items.why: A positive test needs prompt referral.
items.fix: Agree how results are given and book a review.
